name: Putty
lede: Putty is the muddy grey-beige of window glazing compound, a color word that was in print by 1889 and that sits, by our count, on about one painting in nine.

sections.title: The color of the material
sections.body: Paterson defines putty as the muddy grey or brownish-beige of the material, and notes that it is one of the colors in Winifred Nicholson's 1944 *Chart of Colours* [1]. His systematic list files it with the browns [2]. The material itself is old and simple: whiting, pulverized white chalk, is used to make whitewash and putty [3], and slaked lime mixed with water gives lime putty [4].

sections.title: A different putty
sections.body: Coles describes a recipe for making ultramarine in which crushed lapis lazuli is worked into a paste, also called putty, with resin and wax. The paste is kneaded in lye baths, and the blue passes into the water while the impurities stay behind [5]. The best-quality blue leaches out in the first two hours of kneading [5]. The word is the same, but that putty is a blue-making tool, and the color [[putty]] is not related to it.

sections.title: In color systems
sections.body: Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary records putty as first used in 1889, on plate 11 B 2 [6]. ISCC-NBS 1955 places it in blocks 89 and 90, and Ridgway's 1912 *Color Standards* has a near-duplicate called Deep Olive-Buff, a color distance (ΔE) of 2.2 away [6]. Its nearest everyday name is [[tan]], at 5.6 [6].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Putty is one of the most common colors in the archive: 2,572 of the 23,531 paintings carry a color this close, 10.8 percent, as photographed [7]. It is a color of old varnish and weathered ground more than of any one pigment.
